narrativeReportMd:
# NamingSystem R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No hard R4→R6 instance-validation break was found for existing local `NamingSystem` content: no R4 local element was removed, no existing local element cardinality was tightened, and existing local element datatypes are stable. The material migration risk is mostly in the opposite direction and in runtime tooling: R6 adds many optional canonical/governance metadata fields and widens `uniqueId.type` with new required-binding codes that R4 validators and generated enum code will not understand.

## Scope
The comparison used the local R4 and R6 core package StructureDefinitions, package indexes, package metadata, batch manifest entry, and directly relevant ValueSets/CodeSystems. Inherited Resource/DomainResource/Element/BackboneElement changes are excluded from findings under the inherited/base-artifact rule.

## Main migration themes
R4→R6 ingestion is structurally straightforward for existing data, but R6→R4 downgrade is not lossless once R6-only metadata such as `url`, `version`, lifecycle dates, authorship/review contacts, `relatedArtifact`, or `uniqueId.authoritative` is populated. Terminology handling also needs attention because `NamingSystem.uniqueId.type` has new required-binding codes (`iri-stem`, `v2csmnemonic`) and `NamingSystem.type` changed to a different, weaker preferred binding. Several existing elements also acquired more CanonicalResource-like semantics, especially `jurisdiction`, `date`, `description`, and lifecycle metadata.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact local findings are `NamingSystem:ELEMENT_PRESENCE_OR_IDENTITY:NamingSystem:7c8b20` for R6-only metadata fields and `NamingSystem:TERMINOLOGY_BINDING:NamingSystem.uniqueId.type:6d9a91` for the new required-binding codes. These do not invalidate ordinary R4 instances in R6, but they can make R6 instances fail R4 validation or lose important metadata during downgrade.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important where the same element remains structurally valid but the business meaning changes: `jurisdiction` now represents the maintaining authority jurisdiction rather than simply intended use, while `date` and related lifecycle fields separate publication, significant-change, review, approval, and effective-use concepts. Automated transforms can preserve syntax but may not know the correct business interpretation.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most R6 additions are optional and appear to align `NamingSystem` with richer canonical artifact metadata. That is a reasonable major-version evolution, but the same information could have been less disruptive for R6→R4 exchange if represented by standardized cross-version extensions or if old broad semantics were preserved while new semantics were introduced in separate fields. The new `uniqueId.type` codes are clearer than overloading `other`, but they require enum and validator updates.

## Follow-up analysis
Follow-up should cover base Resource/DomainResource/Element changes, datatype changes for newly used complex datatypes, and external terminology expansions for jurisdiction and v2 identifier-type systems.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: No hard R4→R6 instance break was found for local `NamingSystem` fields. The top concerns are lossless R6→R4 downgrade of new metadata, enum/validator handling for new `uniqueId.type` codes, and semantic review for jurisdiction and lifecycle metadata. The main uncertainty is terminology expansion detail for external terminology.hl7.org bindings.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Existing R4 instances should generally validate structurally in R6 after normal version handling, but R6 instances are richer than R4 can natively represent. Migration tooling should preserve R6-only canonical and governance metadata through official cross-version extensions, sidecar metadata, or an R6-native store rather than silently dropping it. Terminology code paths should update generated enums and validation tables for `namingsystem-identifier-type`, and business rules should review `jurisdiction`, `date`, `purpose`, `approvalDate`, `lastReviewDate`, and `effectivePeriod` rather than assuming R4 semantics.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural/cardinality/type comparisons because both assigned StructureDefinitions are present locally and were compared through snapshot and differential elements. Confidence is high for the `uniqueId.type`, `kind`, and `status` code-list comparisons where complete local CodeSystems are present. Confidence is medium for extensible/preferred and external terminology bindings because no live expansion service or official narrative diff was available.

findings.title: R6 adds optional canonical and governance metadata fields that R4 cannot natively carry

oldState.summary: R4 NamingSystem lacked canonical URL/version metadata, business identifiers, lifecycle governance dates, author/reviewer/endorser contacts, relatedArtifact, topic, purpose, copyright, and uniqueId.authoritative.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 local content focused on name/status/kind/date, publisher/contact, categorization, jurisdiction/use context, usage, and unique identifiers. The resource did not have the broader CanonicalResource-style metadata fields that many R6 definitional resources expose.

newState.summary: R6 adds 19 optional local elements, all with min=0, including canonical metadata, lifecycle/governance metadata, related artifacts, and uniqueId.authoritative.

constraints.human: URL should not contain | or # - these characters make processing canonical references problematic
Related artifact can't be depends-on or composed-of
Can't have more than one authoritative identifier for a type/period combination (only one authoritative identifier allowed at any given point of time)

newState.narrativeMd: The added elements are optional, so they do not make old R4 instances invalid in R6. Once populated, however, they are first-class R6 content with no direct R4 element counterparts.

facts.note: All added elements have minimum cardinality 0 in the R6 differential.
Representative added types; other additions use string, boolean, markdown, date, Period, CodeableConcept, or ContactDetail.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 element IDs are additions under the same `NamingSystem` canonical StructureDefinition. No rename or counterpart removal is needed to match them because the R4 differential has no corresponding local element IDs.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4-valid instance remains structurally acceptable with respect to these fields because every added element is optional. The breaking mechanism is reverse-direction and runtime: an R4 parser or generated R4 model that rejects unknown properties cannot accept R6 instances containing these fields, and a downgrade transform cannot represent them in native R4 without extensions or sidecar metadata. Loss of `url`, `version`, lifecycle dates, related artifacts, or authoritative identifier flags can change canonical identification and governance behavior.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is mainly terminology-governance/business integrity rather than direct clinical safety: losing canonical URL/version or authority metadata can cause registries to merge, misidentify, or publish the wrong naming-system record.

justification.inferredGoal: Align NamingSystem with richer canonical artifact metadata and support governance, provenance-like roles, lifecycle dates, related artifacts, and authoritative identifiers.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: This is optional additive R6 content, so it is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of giving `NamingSystem` first-class canonical and governance metadata is reasonable, and all listed additions are optional. Existing R4 instances are preserved in the R4-to-R6 direction; the compatibility concern is that richer R6 instances cannot be represented natively by R4 software.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible base-design alternative is needed to protect R4 instances because the added fields have minimum cardinality 0. Standard R4 extensions, sidecar storage, or conversion rules may be important for R6-to-R4 downgrade, but they do not make this a less-breaking base R6 design alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 extensions or sidecar metadata can preserve downgrade fidelity, but those are conversion mitigations rather than less-breaking R6 base designs.

evidence.detail: R4 differential contains 19 local elements and lacks the R6 canonical/governance additions.
R6 differential adds 19 optional local elements, including `url`, `identifier`, `version`, `versionAlgorithm[x]`, lifecycle/governance fields, `relatedArtifact`, and `uniqueId.authoritative`.
R6 adds local constraints for new content: URL canonical-reference hygiene, relatedArtifact type restrictions, and uniqueness of authoritative identifiers by type/period.

examples.examplesMd: The example is structurally illustrative, not a complete conformance-tested instance. The R6-only fields `url`, `version`, `title`, `relatedArtifact`, and `uniqueId.authoritative` have no native R4 homes.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 expands `NamingSystem` from the R4 shape into a richer canonical/governance artifact. This is not a hard R4→R6 validation break because all added elements are optional. It is still material for conversion and tooling because R6 instances can contain first-class fields that R4 generated classes, JSON schemas, and validators do not recognize. Silent downgrade would lose information that may be used to identify the canonical naming system, distinguish versions, track approval/review/effective dates, and decide which identifier is authoritative.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid instances are not made invalid by these additions. R6-valid instances containing the new fields are not natively representable in R4; strict R4 parsers may reject them as unknown properties, and permissive parsers may drop them. The new local constraints apply only when R6-only fields are used, so they mainly affect R6 authoring and R6→R4 preservation rather than R4→R6 acceptance.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: R4→R6 migration can leave these elements absent unless source metadata exists outside the R4 instance. R6→R4 migration should choose a preservation policy: official cross-version extensions if available, sidecar metadata, an R6-native registry, or explicit documented loss. Test downgrade with instances containing canonical URL/version, lifecycle dates, related artifacts, and `uniqueId.authoritative`; do not rely on unknown-field dropping if round-trip fidelity matters.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The design is only partially backward-compatible. Optional additions avoid old-instance invalidation, but not reverse-direction interoperability. A fully downgrade-compatible approach would have standardized R4 extensions and transform rules for each new field. The tradeoff is that native R6 elements are easier to index, validate, and author than extension-heavy representations.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds optional CanonicalResource-style and governance fields under `NamingSystem`, including `url`, `identifier`, `version`, lifecycle/review metadata, contacts, related artifacts, and `uniqueId.authoritative`. Because all of these additions are min=0, an R4-valid NamingSystem instance is not made invalid in R6. The real concern is reverse-direction fidelity: R6 instances can carry metadata that an R4 model cannot natively represent. That is worth documenting for converters, but it is not a base R4-to-R6 compatibility problem or a design issue that needs renewed standards attention.
keyEvidence: R4 differential local element IDs stop at the R4 fields; R6 differential adds 19 local min=0 elements under the same `NamingSystem` resource.
R6 root and relatedArtifact constraints (`cnl-1`, `nsd-3`, `nsd-4`) apply to R6-only or newly constrained content rather than making existing R4 fields invalid.
Targeted production-use search did not produce sourceable evidence that these optional R6-only metadata additions create a production-critical R4-to-R6 break.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 NamingSystem is trial-use/FMM 1, which softens stability expectations. With no old-valid/new-invalid mechanism and only optional additions, low FMM strongly favors treating this as normal model evolution.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: populated R6-only metadata may be rejected or dropped by strict R4 parsers/converters; no old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 mechanism was found.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base R6 design is needed to preserve R4 instances because the fields are additive and optional. R4 extensions, sidecar metadata, or cross-version transforms can mitigate downgrade loss, but those are migration mechanisms rather than better base R6 designs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: Partially agree: the existing report correctly identifies reverse-direction metadata loss, but its Medium impact framing overstates the R4-to-R6 compatibility concern for optional additions on FMM 1 trial-use content.

findings.title: NamingSystem.uniqueId.type required binding adds iri-stem and v2csmnemonic codes

oldState.summary: R4 required binding to namingsystem-identifier-type|4.0.1 allowed oid, uuid, uri, and other.

binding.description: Identifies the style of unique identifier used to identify a namespace.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R4 CodeSystem is complete and contains `oid`, `uuid`, `uri`, and `other`.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 instances had to choose one of four code values for each `uniqueId.type`.

newState.summary: R6 required binding to namingsystem-identifier-type|6.0.0-ballot4 retains the R4 codes and adds iri-stem and v2csmnemonic.

binding.description: Identifies the style of unique identifier used to identify a namespace.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R6 CodeSystem is complete and adds `iri-stem` for RDF IRI stems and `v2csmnemonic` for HL7 v2 code system mnemonics.

semanticText.short: oid | uuid | uri | iri-stem | v2csmnemonic | other
semanticText.comment: Preferred identifiers for the same identifier type SHOULD NOT overlap by period.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can distinguish identifier styles that R4 could only represent using `other` plus prose.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element path, element ID, cardinality, datatype, and binding name are stable; the local CodeSystem code set changed by adding two codes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: There is no R4→R6 hard break because all R4 codes remain present in R6. The hard validation mechanism appears in the reverse direction: `uniqueId.type` is a required code binding, so an R6 instance using `iri-stem` or `v2csmnemonic` is not valid against the R4 required binding. Generated R4 enums and exhaustive switch statements are also likely to reject or mishandle the new codes at runtime.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is identifier-resolution and terminology-governance failure. Misclassifying a v2 mnemonic or RDF IRI stem as `other` can make registry lookup, canonical matching, or documentation less precise.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent RDF IRI stems and HL7 v2 code system mnemonics explicitly instead of overloading `other`.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: The required code set is widened and retains all R4 codes, so old R4 `uniqueId.type` values remain valid in R6.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The added `iri-stem` and `v2csmnemonic` codes make distinct identifier schemes computable. Because no R4 code is removed, the change does not create a breaking R4-to-R6 validation problem; the main risk is R6 content reaching R4 validators or closed enums.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Continuing to overload `other` with comments or extensions would be a downgrade strategy or a deliberately less expressive R6 model. It is not a backward-compatible alternative for existing R4 instances because those instances already remain valid under the widened R6 binding.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Mapping new R6 codes to `other` helps downgrade but sacrifices machine-processable precision and is not needed to preserve R4 instances.

evidence.detail: R4 binds `NamingSystem.uniqueId.type` with required strength to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/namingsystem-identifier-type|4.0.1`.
R6 binds the same element with required strength to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/namingsystem-identifier-type|6.0.0-ballot4`.
The local complete R6 CodeSystem adds `iri-stem` and `v2csmnemonic`; no R4 codes were removed.

uniqueId.comment: R6 uniqueId.type was iri-stem; downgraded to R4 `other` with explanatory comment.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example preserves R4 validity but is semantically lossy unless a cross-version extension also records the original R6 code.

findings.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.uniqueId.type` is one of the few local places with a direct computable terminology expansion change. R6 keeps all R4 values and adds two more precise values. That is friendly for R4→R6, but not for R6→R4 or for applications that generated closed enums from the R4 required ValueSet.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance using `oid`, `uuid`, `uri`, or `other` remains valid for this binding in R6. An R6 instance using `iri-stem` or `v2csmnemonic` fails R4 required-binding validation because R4 does not contain those codes. Runtime failures are likely in strict deserializers, validation code, database check constraints, and exhaustive enum switches built from R4 definitions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update validators and generated enums to include `iri-stem` and `v2csmnemonic` before accepting R6 content. For R6→R4 downgrade, either map the new codes to `other` with an extension/comment preserving the original code or reject/downscope such instances when precision cannot be lost. Add tests for each R4 code plus both new R6 codes.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change was probably justified because the new codes represent distinct identifier schemes. It was not fully backward-compatible because required bindings are closed. The main compatible alternative, continuing to use `other`, would retain R4 validity but would keep important semantics in prose rather than machine-readable code.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.uniqueId.type` remains a required code with required binding, and R6 retains every R4 code while adding `iri-stem` and `v2csmnemonic`. Existing R4 instances using `oid`, `uuid`, `uri`, or `other` remain valid for this path in R6. The compatibility work is for software with closed R4 enums or R6-to-R4 conversion: new R6 codes cannot be represented in native R4 except by lossy mapping such as `other`. Since the new codes capture real identifier schemes and R6 chose the least disruptive widening pattern, the break is proportionate.
keyEvidence: R6 `CodeSystem-namingsystem-identifier-type` retains those four concepts and adds `iri-stem` and `v2csmnemonic`.
`NamingSystem.uniqueId.type` is min=1, max=1, type `code`, with required binding in both R4 and R6.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use softens the case for standards rework, but this path is central to NamingSystem because `uniqueId` is required and `type` is required within it. That keeps enum/validator migration real while still making Revisit too strong.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: R4-generated closed enums, validators, or switch statements can fail on the two R6-added codes; R6-to-R4 loss occurs if those codes are downgraded to `other`.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 already uses the main less-breaking base design by retaining all R4 codes and widening the value set. Keeping only `other` for these schemes would be more R4-compatible in reverse but would sacrifice computable distinction for RDF IRI stems and HL7 v2 code-system mnemonics.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: Partially agree: the existing report correctly identifies the closed-enum and R6-to-R4 risk, but the High overall impact is somewhat strong because no R4 code was removed and the artifact is FMM 1.

findings.title: NamingSystem.type binding changed from extensible IdentifierType to preferred NamingSystemIdentifierSystemType

oldState.summary: R4 `NamingSystem.type` was a CodeableConcept with extensible binding to the common Identifier Type value set.

binding.description: A coded type for an identifier that can be used to determine which identifier to use for a specific purpose.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 pointed this categorization element at the regular identifier-type value set and asked systems to use a code from that value set when a suitable concept existed.

newState.summary: R6 keeps the CodeableConcept shape but changes the binding to preferred strength and to `namingsystem-identifier-system-type`, composed from v2-0203.

binding.description: A coded type for an identifier that can be used to determine which identifier to use for a specific purpose.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R6 ValueSet composes the entire `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v2-0203` system. The R4 `identifier-type` ValueSet used a named subset of v2-0203 codes with extensible strength.

newState.narrativeMd: The binding is weaker but points to a different, potentially broader system-specific categorization vocabulary.

facts.note: The local R6 package includes the ValueSet compose but not the external v2-0203 CodeSystem file.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element path and datatype are unchanged; only binding strength, binding name extension, and bound ValueSet changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a hard validation break because `CodeableConcept` can carry codes from many systems and R6 weakens the binding from extensible to preferred. The practical risk is conformance and runtime behavior: validators, UI picklists, analytics, or generated terminology helpers that assumed the R4 IdentifierType subset may produce different warnings, suggestions, or search categories under R6. Downgraded R6 instances using broader v2-0203 codes can be represented structurally in R4 but may violate R4 extensible-binding expectations when a suitable R4 code exists.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The main risk is registry categorization and search/filter quality rather than direct safety impact.

justification.inferredGoal: Use a vocabulary tailored to naming-system identifier-system categories and avoid over-constraining a broad categorization field.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: The element shape is unchanged and the binding is weakened to preferred, so this is not an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 base-design break.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: A NamingSystem-specific preferred vocabulary is a plausible lower-pressure conformance direction for this categorization field. The local evidence does not show R4 instances becoming invalid in R6, so the calibration issue is terminology expectation drift rather than avoidable structural breakage.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Keeping the R4 IdentifierType binding as an additional or starter binding may be useful implementation guidance, but it is not required to preserve R4 instances because the `CodeableConcept` datatype remains and preferred binding strength is non-failing. The tradeoff would be validator and UI ambiguity from two partially overlapping picklists.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Retaining the old binding as additional guidance could aid continuity but would introduce dual vocabulary expectations rather than solve an instance-compatibility break.

evidence.detail: R4 binding strength is extensible and valueSet is `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/identifier-type`.
R6 binding strength is preferred and valueSet is `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/namingsystem-identifier-system-type`.

examples.examplesMd: The example is structurally valid as a CodeableConcept in both versions, but an R4 validator applying the extensible `identifier-type` subset may warn if the code is outside the R4 ValueSet and a suitable in-set code is expected.

findings.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.type` did not change shape, but it changed terminology contract. R4 used the common IdentifierType ValueSet with extensible strength. R6 uses a NamingSystem-specific ValueSet with preferred strength. Implementers who treated the R4 binding as a stable picklist or code-generation source need to revisit their terminology assumptions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Existing R4 instances are unlikely to become invalid solely because the R6 binding is weaker. R6 instances can still be serialized in R4 because the element remains CodeableConcept, but conformance behavior is not equivalent: R4 validators may issue extensible-binding warnings for R6-preferred codes outside the old subset, while R6 validators may no longer issue the same pressure to choose from the old IdentifierType set.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not blindly reuse R4 `NamingSystem.type` enum/picklist logic for R6. Update terminology services, UI filters, and analytics to use the R6 binding. For downgrade, preserve the Coding as-is where possible and record any R4 validation warnings; if a specific R4 IdentifierType mapping exists, consider adding that coding as an additional translation rather than replacing the original.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been made more compatible by retaining the old binding as an additional/starter binding or by introducing the new ValueSet with preferred guidance while keeping the old extensible binding for conformance. The tradeoff is that implementers would have to reconcile two partially overlapping category vocabularies.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: A terminology expansion service would improve confidence about the exact overlap between the old IdentifierType subset and the new NamingSystemIdentifierSystemType ValueSet.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.type` keeps the same optional `CodeableConcept` shape. R6 changes the binding target and weakens the strength from extensible to preferred. That can alter UI picklists, validator advice, or analytics expectations, but it does not make R4 content invalid and it reduces rather than increases formal conformance pressure. For this path, the change is terminology guidance drift rather than a material compatibility break.
keyEvidence: R4 `NamingSystem.type` is 0..1 `CodeableConcept` with extensible binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/identifier-type`.
R6 `NamingSystem.type` is still 0..1 `CodeableConcept`, with preferred binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/namingsystem-identifier-system-type`.
The local R6 ValueSet composes `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v2-0203`; the local R4 IdentifierType ValueSet used an explicit v2-0203 subset.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use lowers the stability concern, and the binding strength decrease means the change should not be treated as a hard conformance break.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: warning-level: terminology suggestions and warnings may change, but the element shape is unchanged and R6 weakens the binding to preferred.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have retained the old IdentifierType binding as additional guidance, but that would mainly preserve familiar picklists while creating dual vocabulary expectations. It is not needed to preserve R4 instances.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: Disagree: the existing report's Medium impact appears too high for an optional CodeableConcept whose binding is weakened; the no-less-breaking-alternative conclusion is mostly acceptable.

findings.title: NamingSystem.jurisdiction now describes maintainer authority jurisdiction and is deprecated in favor of useContext jurisdiction

oldState.summary: R4 jurisdiction represented legal/geographic regions where the naming system was intended to be used.

binding.description: Countries and regions within which this artifact is targeted for use.

semanticText.short: Intended jurisdiction for naming system (if applicable)
semanticText.definition: A legal or geographic region in which the naming system is intended to be used.
semanticText.comment: It may be possible for the naming system to be used in jurisdictions other than those for which it was originally designed or intended.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 made `jurisdiction` a targeting/use-context concept: where the naming system was intended to be used.

newState.summary: R6 jurisdiction represents the legal/geographic region of the authority maintaining the resource; intended/additional jurisdictions are directed to useContext with a jurisdiction code.

binding.description: Countries and regions within which this artifact is targeted for use.

semanticText.short: Jurisdiction of the authority that maintains the naming system (if applicable)
semanticText.definition: A legal or geographic region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating. In general, the jurisdiction is also found in the useContext.
semanticText.comment: DEPRECATION NOTE: For consistency, implementations are encouraged to migrate to using the new 'jurisdiction' code in the useContext element.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 narrows the primary meaning to maintainer authority jurisdiction and recommends representing jurisdictional applicability through `useContext`.

facts.oldValue: Intended jurisdiction for naming system (if applicable)
facts.newValue: Jurisdiction of the authority that maintains the naming system (if applicable)

facts.oldValue: A legal or geographic region in which the naming system is intended to be used.
facts.newValue: A legal or geographic region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating.
Deprecation note recommends using useContext.code = http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/usage-context-type#jurisdiction with useContext.valueCodeableConcept for jurisdiction.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element path, datatype, cardinality, and extensible binding strength are stable; the semantic text and ValueSet canonical changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The validation mechanism is semantic rather than structural. Existing R4 instances with `jurisdiction` remain syntactically valid in R6, but a value that meant 'intended region of use' in R4 can be interpreted as 'jurisdiction of the maintaining authority' in R6. Search, registry filtering, governance review, and publication logic can therefore make different decisions even though validation passes.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Jurisdiction drives registry discoverability and governance. Misinterpreting intended-use jurisdiction as maintainer jurisdiction can cause incorrect publication or filtering decisions.

justification.inferredGoal: Separate authority/stewardship jurisdiction from applicability/use-context jurisdiction and align definitional resources on useContext for contextual targeting.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Preserve the R4 intended-use meaning of `jurisdiction`, deprecate it for new targeting, and add or use a separate field for maintainer authority jurisdiction.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating maintainer authority jurisdiction from applicability jurisdiction is a reasonable R6 goal. Reusing the existing `jurisdiction` path for a different primary meaning, however, creates a still-valid-but-behaviorally-different migration hazard that could likely have been avoided with a separate maintainer-jurisdiction representation and clearer deprecation guidance.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep `NamingSystem.jurisdiction` with its R4 intended-use semantics while recommending `useContext` jurisdiction for new contextual targeting and adding an optional maintainer-authority jurisdiction element if that distinct fact must be captured. The cost is duplicate or legacy representations that may persist indefinitely, but that tradeoff is moderate compared with silently changing the meaning of populated R4 fields.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The alternative leaves legacy and useContext jurisdiction representations in circulation, but avoids silent reinterpretation of existing data.

evidence.detail: R4 definition says jurisdiction is the region where the naming system is intended to be used.
evidence.quote: A legal or geographic region in which the naming system is intended to be used.

evidence.detail: R6 definition says jurisdiction is the region where the maintaining authority operates and includes a deprecation note directing migration to useContext jurisdiction.
evidence.quote: Jurisdiction of the authority that maintains the naming system

evidence.detail: The binding canonical changes from `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/jurisdiction` to `http://terminology.hl7.org/ValueSet/jurisdiction` with extensible strength retained.

examples.examplesMd: If the R4 value represented intended use, migration should consider moving or copying it into `useContext` with code `jurisdiction`. Keep `NamingSystem.jurisdiction` only when it also represents the maintainer authority's jurisdiction.

findings.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.jurisdiction` is a same-path semantic change. It still looks like the same repeating CodeableConcept, which makes automated migration tempting, but the R6 text changes what the field is supposed to mean and marks the old style as deprecated in favor of `useContext`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: There is no direct old-valid/new-invalid validation mechanism. The compatibility issue is still-valid-but-behaviorally-different: a value can pass both R4 and R6 validation while being interpreted differently by repositories, search filters, and governance workflows.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review every populated R4 `jurisdiction`. If it records intended usage/applicability, map it to `useContext` using `http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/usage-context-type#jurisdiction`. If it records the maintaining authority's jurisdiction, it can remain in `NamingSystem.jurisdiction`. When both meanings apply, duplicate deliberately and document the decision.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change improves cross-resource consistency but reuses an existing element for a different primary meaning. A backward-compatible alternative would add a separate maintainer-jurisdiction element and leave `jurisdiction` as intended-use. That would avoid ambiguity but would not converge with the R6 useContext pattern.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The R6 jurisdiction ValueSet canonical points to terminology.hl7.org; a full external expansion comparison would improve confidence that code membership is otherwise equivalent.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.jurisdiction` is the concerning same-path change in this report. R4 describes the field as the legal or geographic region where the naming system is intended to be used. R6 describes it as the jurisdiction of the authority maintaining the resource and directs implementations toward `useContext` with a jurisdiction code. Existing instances can still validate, but a populated R4 value can be silently reinterpreted unless a migrator decides whether it describes intended use, maintaining authority, or both. Because a plausible base design could have preserved the old meaning while adding a separate maintainer-jurisdiction representation, this deserves renewed review despite the low FMM.
keyEvidence: R4 definition: `NamingSystem.jurisdiction` is a region in which the naming system is intended to be used.
R6 definition: `NamingSystem.jurisdiction` is a region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating.
R6 comment includes a deprecation note encouraging migration to `useContext` with `usage-context-type#jurisdiction`; cardinality and datatype remain 0..* `CodeableConcept`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use softens the stability burden and prevents assuming broad production impact. It does not eliminate concern because jurisdiction can drive governance/regulatory filtering and migration is expert-dependent for each populated value.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: the same data remains syntactically valid but the path's intended meaning changes from intended use to maintaining authority jurisdiction.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have deprecated `jurisdiction` for new targeting while preserving its R4 intended-use meaning, then added an optional maintainer-authority jurisdiction element or pattern. The tradeoff is duplicate jurisdiction representations and a longer transition, but it avoids silent reinterpretation of existing data.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: Agree: the existing report correctly identifies a semantic migration hazard and a plausible less-breaking base design, though low FMM keeps the concern focused on populated jurisdiction workflows rather than the entire resource.

findings.title: Lifecycle metadata semantics shifted around date, purpose, publisher, and review/effective dates

oldState.summary: R4 `date` definition described when the naming system was published; `description` could include why the naming system was built; R4 lacked separate purpose, approval, review, and effective-period fields.

semanticText.definition: The date (and optionally time) when the naming system was published.
semanticText.comment: Description could capture details such as why the naming system was built.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 compressed several lifecycle and rationale concepts into broader fields such as `date` and `description`.

newState.summary: R6 `date` is when the naming system was last significantly changed; R6 adds purpose, approvalDate, lastReviewDate, effectivePeriod, and adjusts publisher/steward wording.

semanticText.definition: The date (and optionally time) when the naming system was last significantly changed.
semanticText.comment: Date may be absent on draft content until publication; purpose and lifecycle fields carry rationale and approval/review/effective-use concepts.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 separates publication/review/approval/effective-use/rationale concepts that may have been conflated in R4 instances.

facts.oldValue: The date (and optionally time) when the naming system was published.
facts.newValue: The date (and optionally time) when the naming system was last significantly changed.

facts.oldValue: Description can capture details such as why the naming system was built.
facts.newValue: R6 description comment no longer lists 'why the naming system was built'; R6 adds `NamingSystem.purpose` for why the naming system is needed/designed.

facts.oldValue: The name of the organization or individual that published the naming system.
facts.newValue: The name of the organization or individual responsible for the release and ongoing maintenance of the naming system.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The primary changed element is the same `NamingSystem.date` path. Related semantic changes are local R6 additions and text changes that partition lifecycle metadata previously represented in broader R4 fields.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The existing `date` element remains required `dateTime`, so there is no syntax or cardinality break. The risk is semantic: systems that used R4 `date` as publication date may sort, display, or audit R6 records incorrectly because R6 makes it the last significant-change date and adds separate lifecycle fields. R6 lifecycle fields also cannot be represented natively in R4, so downgrade can lose the distinction between publication, approval, review, effective use, and rationale.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is mainly governance, audit, and publication workflow accuracy.

justification.inferredGoal: Make NamingSystem lifecycle metadata more explicit and align it with canonical artifact governance patterns.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `date` aligned with the R4 publication/change wording and add a separate last-significant-change or lifecycle date element.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 lifecycle goal is reasonable, and R4 `date` already mixed publication wording with requirements to change when business version, status, or substantive content changes. A less-breaking field split is possible, but its model and cross-resource consistency costs are material enough that the R6 approach is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A partial alternative would preserve the old `date` semantics for systems treating it as publication date and introduce a new native element for last significant change, approval, review, or effective-use distinctions. That would protect common historical interpretations, but implementers would need to reconcile closely related date fields, and deprecated or redundant lifecycle representations could accumulate over time.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This would reduce migration ambiguity but create parallel lifecycle date fields and weaken consistency with the broader canonical-resource date model.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `date` as when the naming system was published.
evidence.quote: when the naming system was published

evidence.detail: R6 defines `date` as when the naming system was last significantly changed.

evidence.locator: differential.element[id in NamingSystem.purpose, approvalDate, lastReviewDate, effectivePeriod]
evidence.detail: R6 adds separate optional lifecycle/rationale elements not present in R4.
R4 description comment allowed description to include why the naming system was built; R6 removes that example and adds `purpose` for the why/rationale concept.

migrationExampleJson.purpose: Defined to provide a stable namespace for local registry identifiers.

examples.examplesMd: In R6, these values have distinct meanings. In R4, only `date` and broad text fields are available, so a downgrade needs extensions or external metadata to avoid flattening the distinctions.

findings.narrativeMd: Several same-looking lifecycle fields are not semantically interchangeable across versions. The most important is `date`: the type and cardinality stay the same, but R6 says it is the last significant-change date rather than the publication date. R6 also adds explicit homes for rationale, approval, review, and effective-use period that R4 implementations may have stored in `description`, `usage`, or external registry metadata.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No R4 instance becomes invalid because `date` remains required `dateTime`. The compatibility issue is still-valid-but-behaviorally-different and R6-to-R4 information loss. Publication workflows, audit screens, cache invalidation, and version-selection logic that read `date` need to check which version semantics they are processing.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: During R4→R6 migration, decide whether each R4 `date` value is actually publication date, last significant-change date, or both. If source systems have separate approval/review/effective metadata, populate the new R6 fields rather than leaving it embedded in description. For R6→R4, preserve the extra lifecycle fields using extensions or sidecar metadata; if flattening into `description` or `usage`, mark the transform as lossy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change probably improves semantic clarity but reinterprets an existing required element. A backward-compatible alternative would have introduced a new last-change element and retained the old publication-date definition. That would reduce migration ambiguity but at the cost of more fields and less alignment with the R6 canonical-resource lifecycle model.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `NamingSystem.date` remains required `dateTime`, so this is not a structural break. The first sentence changes from publication date in R4 to last significant-change date in R6, while R6 adds separate lifecycle fields such as `approvalDate`, `lastReviewDate`, `effectivePeriod`, and `purpose`. Migration can require judgment if an R4 registry treated `date` as publication date only. However, R4 already required the date to change when business version, status, or substantive content changed, so the R6 wording is partly a clarification and alignment with canonical-resource lifecycle metadata rather than an arbitrary reinterpretation.
keyEvidence: R4 `NamingSystem.date` is min=1, max=1, type `dateTime`, defined as when the naming system was published, with text requiring changes when business version, status, or substantive content changes.
R6 `NamingSystem.date` is still min=1, max=1, type `dateTime`, defined as when the naming system was last significantly changed.
R6 differential adds optional lifecycle/rationale fields including `purpose`, `approvalDate`, `lastReviewDate`, and `effectivePeriod`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use softens the case for Revisit. The field is required and can affect audit or publication workflows, so the semantic migration is real, but the old wording already contained change-date behavior.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: existing instances validate, but date-driven audit, sorting, publication, or cache logic may need version-aware interpretation; R6-to-R4 loss is possible for the new lifecycle fields.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have kept `date` as publication date and added a new last-significant-change field, but that would create overlapping lifecycle dates and diverge from the broader canonical-resource pattern. Given the R4 text already mixed publication and change semantics, the R6 design appears proportionate.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: Partially agree: the existing report correctly flags a semantic migration burden and partial alternative, but the concern is moderated by the R4 change-date wording and low FMM.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The R6 StructureDefinition is present and retains the same canonical URL, id/name, kind `resource`, type `NamingSystem`, baseDefinition `DomainResource`, derivation `specialization`, and `abstract=false`. The computable status changed from draft to active, which is noted separately as non-breaking maturity/governance information.

All existing local R4 element cardinalities are unchanged in R6: required elements such as `name`, `status`, `kind`, `date`, `uniqueId`, `uniqueId.type`, and `uniqueId.value` remain required; all R6-added elements have min=0.

Existing local element datatypes are unchanged. New R6 elements introduce additional datatypes, including `Identifier`, `Coding`, `RelatedArtifact`, `ContactDetail`, `Period`, and `date`, but no existing R4 local element type was removed or replaced.

No existing local `NamingSystem` element is a `Reference`, and no reference target list changed. `relatedArtifact` is a new complex datatype element; its internal reference/attachment behavior is a datatype concern outside this local resource comparison.

The required `NamingSystem.status` PublicationStatus and `NamingSystem.kind` NamingSystemType bindings point to versioned R6 ValueSets but local complete CodeSystems show the same code sets as R4. Separate findings cover the material `uniqueId.type` and `type` binding changes.

Existing local root error constraints `nsd-1` and `nsd-2` are retained. No existing R4-valid instance pattern was found to become R6-invalid through a tightened local error constraint. New constraints involving R6-only fields are covered under the metadata-addition finding; the machine-name warning change is listed as a notable non-breaking change.
No local fixed, pattern, or default value constraints were identified for `NamingSystem` elements in either version.

No computable maxLength, minValue, maxValue, or regex value-limit tightening was found on existing local elements. `copyrightLabel` text describes a short string expectation but no computable maxLength is present in the inspected ElementDefinition.

`NamingSystem.status` remains the local modifier element. R6 explicitly records `isModifier=false` on many non-modifier elements, equivalent to absent/false in R4. Inherited modifierExtension behavior is out of scope.

No material summary-flag change was found on existing local elements. R6-added elements introduce their own summary participation, especially canonical metadata, but this is part of the element-addition finding.
No local slicing or slice discriminator changes were found for `NamingSystem`.

JSON/XML representation of existing local elements is unchanged. R6-only properties create strict-parser and downgrade risks covered by findings. Inherited serialization details from base Element/Resource definitions are out of scope.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: StructureDefinition maturity/status changed from draft to active
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This is metadata about the definition artifact, not an instance content-model change. It does not invalidate R4 `NamingSystem` instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The status change may affect governance expectations and confidence in the R6 model. The R6 package is still a ballot build marked not-for-publication, so consumers should not treat it as final release stability.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Machine-name warning changed from nsd-0 to cnl-0 and now expects at least two characters
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The constraint remains a warning, not an error, and affects only unusual one-character names or systems that elevate warnings to failures. `NamingSystem.name` cardinality and datatype did not change.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Code generators and strict validation pipelines should test short names. A one-character R4 name such as `A` satisfied the R4 warning expression but does not satisfy the R6 `cnl-0` expression.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 clarifies that period end represents identifier deprecation
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element type and cardinality are unchanged and no new computable invariant was added to `period` itself. Existing R4 data remains structurally valid.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Business logic should interpret an ended `uniqueId.period` as a signal that the identifier should no longer be used once the end date is reached. Older systems may have treated it only as a general validity range.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Required code sets for status and kind appear unchanged despite versioned ValueSet URLs
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Local complete CodeSystems for `publication-status` and `namingsystem-type` have the same codes in R4 and R6. The binding URLs are versioned to the R6 package, but no code removal or addition was found for these two required bindings.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Validators should update canonical version references but should not need data transforms for existing `status` or `kind` codes.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited/base-definition changes were intentionally excluded from local findings under the scope rule. They can still affect generated classes, inherited validation, summary serialization, language binding, contained-resource rules, and extension behavior for every resource including `NamingSystem`.
R6 adds `NamingSystem.relatedArtifact`. Its internal representation, allowed reference/attachment forms, and type-code changes should be analyzed in the datatype report rather than duplicated here.
The `jurisdiction` binding canonical changes to terminology.hl7.org. A full expansion comparison would confirm whether code membership is equivalent to the R4 jurisdiction ValueSet.

R6 `NamingSystem.type` uses a ValueSet composed from v2-0203. The R6 core package did not include the external CodeSystem file, so exact expansion overlap with the R4 IdentifierType subset should be verified by terminology analysis.
